**Verdict:** Paul Graham would almost certainly say this is a bad startup to work on. He'd grant that students would pay for it. What he'd object to is that the product sells the customer a way to skip the thinking that writing exists to force. Working on that is a bad problem, and it doesn't make the buyer's life better.

**Based on:** follows from what he said. Confidence is high that he'd call it bad for the world, because one of his stated rules applies directly and he's repeated it across several sources. It's medium that he'd tell the founders not to build it, because that part rests on one analogy.

**How we get there**
1. **The nearest case he wrote about.** In *Writes and Write-Nots* (2024, https://paulgraham.com/writes.html) he describes exactly this "escape valve": "You could pay someone to write for you, like JFK, or plagiarize, like MLK, but if you couldn't buy or steal words, you had to write them yourself." Then: "Not anymore. AI has blown this world open. Almost all pressure to write has dissipated. You can have AI do it for you, both in school and at work." ([[web-14f0078fb455]]). An AI admissions-essay company sells that escape valve to students, the group he names.
2. **The rule behind it.** He thinks writing is thinking. "Yes, it's bad. The reason is something I mentioned earlier: writing is thinking." The result is "a world of thinks and think-nots" ([[web-14f0078fb455]]; [[thinking/pg]]). He calls that outcome bad without hedging.
3. **Why this case falls under the rule.** The product's whole value is that the student doesn't do the thinking. Its natural market is also the teenagers who would otherwise have had to learn to write.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Demand isn't enough when the problem is bad.** He takes this position on brand: "pushing people's brand buttons is just not a good problem to work on, and it's hard to do good work without a good problem." ([[web-35ed22df6265]], https://paulgraham.com/brandage.html). Making money from customers' worst incentives is the same kind of business.
- **It's a tool for gaming the system.** He says young founders were trained by school to look for the trick: "The reason young founders go through the motions of starting a startup is because that is what they have been trained to do for their whole lives up to this point." He also says "Starting a startup is where gaming the system stops working." ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 8:08, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=488s; @ 11:00). This startup would turn the trick into a product.
- **Customers have to come out better off.** "The only way they can become powerful is to make customers' lives better." ([[web-19ac0b6d18d2]], https://paulgraham.com/powerful.html), and "the key is not exploitation but empathy." ([[web-278ac10fa14b]], https://paulgraham.com/earn.html). A student who gets into college on an essay they couldn't have written has been made worse off where it matters to him.
- **His idea of good work.** "One should help people, and take care of the world. Those two are obvious. But is there anything else? When I ask that, the answer that pops up is Make good new things." ([[web-3c8cb136189b]], https://paulgraham.com/do.html). This product is a new delivery method for something old: buying words.

**The tension, resolved his way:** his main test is "you have to have something people want. And you only prosper to the extend that you do." ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 12:43). Students clearly want this, so he'd expect it to get users. But in his 2026 essays he puts making customers' lives better above simply extracting money from them: "Squeezing every last penny out of customers is a distraction" ([[web-19ac0b6d18d2]]). On that ranking the demand doesn't save the idea.

**What would change his answer:**
- **A tutor instead of a ghostwriter.** If the product made students write and think better, so that they write the essay themselves, it would fit his "always be learning" view and he'd probably like it.
- **Killing the essay as a gate.** If the real effect were to make admissions essays worthless as a filter, he might welcome that outcome while still disliking the business that caused it. That's the difference that could break the inference.

Two caveats. The vault notes that he's a professional essayist with a personal stake in valuing writing. Separately, and not in the vault, he has written elsewhere about school teaching kids to hack tests, which points the same way.

## Probably not, at least not on the strength of that year

**Verdict:** Probably not. Paul Graham funds people who build things, and a year spent on a business plan with no product is close to his textbook example of going through the motions instead of doing the essential thing. He'd see the year as wasted at best, and at worst as a sign that the founder thinks a startup is a story told to investors.

**Based on:** This follows from what he said. Confidence is high: the same rule shows up in at least three of his sources. He never talks about a founder who spent a year on a plan, but he does attack business plan competitions directly.

**How we get there**
1. **The closest case he addressed is business plan competitions.** In *How Universities Should Prepare Founders* (Aug 2026, https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html) he calls them "not merely useless but positively misleading. It trains founders to think that fundraising is the essential step in starting a startup." His alternative: "Instead of thinking about startups without building anything, they should be building things without thinking about whether they'll turn into startups."
2. **The rule underneath it:** users are the test, and you persuade them with something that works. "The people you need to impress are users, not investors, and the way you impress them is with prototypes, not words." Someone who writes a business plan is impressing investors with words.
3. **Why this founder fits the rule:** a year of planning is the same mistake as the competition, only bigger and done for real. It's thinking about a startup without building anything.

**Why he'd say it**
- **What he looks for in founders:** "They want people who are good at building things and have a habit of doing it." A year with nothing built shows the opposite habit.
- **He thinks you learn by doing:** "the best way to learn how to start a startup is to try and start it. You may not be successful, but you'll learn faster if you just do it." (*Before the Startup*, 2014, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=2016s)
- **He calls going through the motions "playing house":** those founders "have neglected the one thing that's actually essential which is to make something people want." (same talk, @ 7:32)
- **The plan will be out of date anyway:** "startups' ideas are very mutable" (2026 interview, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=1227s). Detailed planning for an idea that will change is mostly wasted.
- **Seibel says the same thing for YC as a whole:** "spending all that time on a pitch deck is not as valuable as spending your time building anything that you can give to a customer" (2019).

**What would change his answer:** In the end he backs the founder, not the idea or what they did in the past. If this person is otherwise "formidable", meaning someone who "gets what they want in any situation", and they also have a record of building things, he'd treat the plan year as a mistake to drop, not as a reason to reject them. That's especially true if they now build something quickly. The vault has nothing from PG saying a plan-first approach is fine for regulated or hard-tech companies. Seibel allows that those can't launch as fast, but that's his view, not PG's.

Two caveats from the vault: PG's case against business plans comes from YC's co-founder, who calls YC itself the only real startup class. And he admits he has never been clear on what a "lean startup" is, so don't read this as him endorsing that particular method.

**Verdict:** Paul Graham would think it's a mistake. He'd want the co-founders in one place, and that place should be Silicon Valley, at least for a while. A fully remote team spread across time zones gives up the things he thinks make startups work: good peers, chance meetings, and the speed that comes from people pushing each other.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: medium). The vault has nothing from PG about remote work or time zones. This answer applies his views on location and co-founders, which he's stated in several sources.

**How we get there**
1. His closest case is the question "should I move to Silicon Valley?" His answer: "Yes, you should. You can go there for a bit and then come back, but you should at least go." ([Stockholm talk, 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=36s) @ 0:36)
2. The rule behind it, from his thinking page: **go where the best people are**, because "You'll become like whoever you work with." ([When To Do What You Love](https://paulgraham.com/when.html))
3. Every reason he gives for being in one place is about people being physically near each other. A team split across time zones has none of that, not even between the founders. So the case falls under his rule, and it's arguably worse than the "stay home in Stockholm" case he was answering.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Chance meetings matter most.** "if you're working on something ambitious, there's nothing in the world that's better than serendipitous meetings with people who are working on the same stuff." ([@ 3:20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=200s)) He also suspects that "planned meetings lop off the outliers." A remote team across time zones runs entirely on planned calls.
- **Being close makes you faster.** "Things also tend to move faster in the big centers because the people are better, they're more confident, and that's more decisive. They also tend to egg one another on." ([@ 3:53](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=233s)) Founders who can only talk during a few overlapping hours can't push each other along like that.
- **You test a co-founder by working with them.** "the only way to tell for sure if someone will be good to work with is to work with them. Apple and Microsoft were just the last of many projects their founders had worked on together." ([How Universities Should Prepare Founders, 2026](https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html))
- **Where you are changes you.** "the biggest advantage of moving to one of these centers is not what it does for you, but what it does to you." ([@ 8:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=499s))
- **Altman agrees from YC's side.** "it used to be very heretical that YC told people they had to move to San Francisco. And looking back, it was clearly right." (Altman, July 2026, @ 16:25) This is Altman speaking, not PG.

**What he's done:** He invested in English founders, and one of those companies moved to Silicon Valley (@ 12:47). Beyond the vault: for most of its history YC has expected founders to be in the Bay Area during the batch, and PG has written elsewhere that founders should work together in person. That's not in the vault, so I can't quote it.

**What would change his answer:**
- He admits he doesn't know *why* chance meetings matter so much, and offers only guesses (@ 2:47). Strong evidence that remote teams match co-located ones would weaken his argument at its base.
- In September 2026 he said AI has changed almost nothing about how startups work. So "AI tools make remote fine" probably wouldn't move him.
- Altman is less sure the advice will hold for the next ten years. If PG ever changes his mind, that doubt is the likely opening.

My own take, kept separate from his view: plenty of good remote companies exist now, and the vault's sources skew toward people who built their careers on the Bay Area.

**Verdict:** Almost certainly no. Paul Graham would tell you not to take a large seed investment from Google, at least not one that ties you to them strategically. His rule is to make your company more powerful, and you can't easily do that when the giant that could absorb you also owns a big piece of you.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: medium). Nothing in the vault mentions strategic or corporate investors. I searched the wiki and the 24 raw sources, and the only Google mentions are about search being replaced by AI and Googlers as recruits. So this answer comes from his nearest rules, not from a quote on this situation.

**How we get there**
1. **The nearest case he did address** is a startup that depends on a bigger company. His office-hours question is "In what ways is the current idea being held back by other companies?" He says much of strategy is "finding ways not to be held back by other companies." About companies that rely on model providers, he asks "how easy it would be for them to engulf you, or even your customers." (Making Startups Powerful, 2026, https://paulgraham.com/powerful.html)
2. **The rule behind it** is in the thinking page (`wiki/thinking/pg.md`): "what would make this company more powerful?" Owning the customer relationship and the money flow, and being upstream, make you powerful. Being "a mere component supplier" living "in a … box created by another company" does not.
3. **How a big Google stake fits the rule:** it makes your most likely acquirer, partner or competitor an insider at the point where you have the least power. It also tends to push you to build for Google's ecosystem, which is exactly the box he tells founders to escape. He would likely add that wanting the big check is the "cowering" he describes: "the reason the idea is complicated is often fear."

**Why he'd say it**
- **Users are the test, not investors:** "Fundraising is merely a necessary evil. The people you need to impress are users, not investors" (How Universities Should Prepare Founders, 2026, https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html). A famous name on the cap table doesn't change the one thing that matters.
- **Keep options open when unsure:** "The less sure you are about what to do, the more important it is to choose options that give you more options in the future. I call this 'staying upwind.'" (When To Do What You Love, https://paulgraham.com/when.html). A seed company is as unsure as companies get, and a strategic investor narrows your future options: other acquirers, other investors, other platforms.
- **A seed company barely needs the money:** he says you can still start on little money and should adjust spending to what you have (`wiki/startups/fundamentals/can-you-still-start-a-startup-on-little-money.md`). A big check solves a problem a seed-stage company mostly doesn't have.
- **Leverage:** this point comes from Dalton Caldwell and Michael Seibel, not Paul Graham. They say leverage is being able to walk away, and that it's built before the negotiation. Taking a strategic's money early gives some of that away to the one party that most wants it.

**What he's done (not in the vault):** I recall YC's long-standing advice that strategic investors at the seed stage cause signaling problems. Other acquirers and VCs read the stake as Google having first claim on you, and the terms sometimes include rights of first refusal on an acquisition. I can't quote him on this from the vault, so treat it as background.

**What would change his answer:** if Google's money comes with no strings, meaning a small check with no board seat, no information rights, no right of first refusal and no exclusivity, it's just money. Then his test is whether it makes the company more powerful and better for customers. The other case is a company that is a Google component and always will be. Even then, he'd push you to find a way to own the customer relationship rather than lock in the dependence.

The vault has nothing on this exact question, so if you want a better answer, Paul Graham's fundraising essays (e.g. "How to Raise Money", "A Fundraising Survival Guide") would be the sources to add.

**Verdict:** Paul Graham would most likely be unimpressed. To him a patent is legal protection, not the thing that makes a startup succeed. He'd ask what the growth rate is and whether users actually want the product. If the patent is doing the work that a better product should be doing, he'd see it as a warning sign.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: medium). The vault has nothing from PG about patents. The answer comes from his views on what makes startups win and what makes them powerful.

**How we get there**
1. **Users are the test, not protection.** He says a startup is where gaming the system stops working: "you have to have something people want. And you only prosper to the extend that you do." ([yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ @ 12:43](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=763s)). He also says tricks "are an order of magnitude less important than solving the real problem" (@ 13:17). A patent keeps rivals out, but it doesn't make anyone want the product.
2. **His idea of power is earned from customers.** "Newly founded startups are too weak to force anything on anyone. The only way they can become powerful is to make customers' lives better." Every power move he recommends "has to make things better for the customer" ([powerful.html](https://paulgraham.com/powerful.html)). The moats he names are network effects, owning the customer relationship, going full stack and getting upstream. Patents aren't on the list. A patent blocks competitors by force without making anyone's life better, which is the opposite of what he looks for.
3. **He expects other advantages to wear away.** "Making the substantive differences between products disappear is what technology naturally tends to do" ([brandage.html](https://paulgraham.com/brandage.html)). And "a company that grows fast enough can shut out potential competitors" ([superlinear.html](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html)). On his view, a startup holds off competitors by growing fast, not through a legal barrier that someone can design around.

**Why he'd say it**
- **He backs founders, not assets.** He says "startups' ideas are very mutable" ([yt-5bxp78i96S8 @ 20:27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=1227s)). He wants "people who are good at building things and have a habit of doing it." A patent ties the company to one idea, while he expects the idea to change.
- **His first question is the growth rate.** "I always begin by asking founders their growth rate. It shows whether they've built the right thing." A patent says nothing about that.
- **YC's early view of patent law:** Jessica Livingston, not PG, recalls that the first batch's guest speakers included "lawyers talking about patent law which of course when you're early stage startups not the like most important thing" ([yt-6u4JVz7iQTY @ 20:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6u4JVz7iQTY&t=1224s)).
- **Not in the vault:** his 2006 essay "Are Software Patents Evil?" isn't in the vault. As I recall it, he treats patents mostly as a defensive tool and something acquirers check for, and says startups shouldn't count on them for protection. The real protection is being better and faster than competitors.

**What would change his answer:** a patent that comes out of real technical work and protects a product users clearly want and are already adopting fast. Biotech or hard tech could qualify, and he says the hard part of a startup comes from studying "molecular biology" and similar fields. In that case the patent is a side effect of something good, and he'd judge the company on the product and its growth. What would still bother him is a patent offered *as* the main advantage. That suggests the founders think they'll win by blocking competitors rather than by being better.

**Verdict:** Paul Graham would say don't do it. A startup is about the slowest and most painful way to become famous, and fame-seekers usually don't survive the years of hard work before anyone notices them. He'd tell the founder to find a problem they actually care about and make something people want. If the startup works, the recognition comes as a side effect.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: high). He has never talked about "fame" in so many words, but in September 2026 he addressed the closest case, founders who want a startup for prestige or to seem cool.

**How we get there**
1. **The nearest case he addressed:** people who apply to YC for prestige. "It was quite early on in YC's history when people started applying to YC for the prestige, right?" and "these people trying to get YC trying to do YC as a credential, they had no idea what they were asking for." ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=498s) @ 8:18, 8:52)
2. **The rules behind it, from his thinking page:**
   - He's against choosing work for status or pay.
   - He puts curiosity over careerism.
   - He thinks users are the real test, so you can't game a startup.
3. **Why fame falls under those rules:** fame is a status reward that arrives late and only if the company wins. Prestige and "seeming cool" have exactly that property, so his answer carries over.

**Why he'd say it**
- **It's the least efficient route.** "If you want to seem cool, like starting a startup is just about the least efficient way to do it." "And you won't seem cool for years of years of brutal hardness before anyone will think you're cool." ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=532s) @ 8:52, 9:23). The vault rates this exchange medium confidence because the speaker turns aren't fully clear in the transcript.
- **There's no easy path.** "With startups, there's no easy majors" and "It's really rough if you're not very very hard working and clever and determined." (@ 8:18, 8:52)
- **A distant reward doesn't keep founders going.** He says founders need real ambition, because "honestly being dutiful is not enough." On a normal day, though, what drives them isn't the big payoff: "You know what actually motivates founders day-to-day? The fear of failure." He also says "you're not thinking I got to deal with this because if I deal with it I'll become a billionaire." (@ 5:32, 6:05). Fame, like wealth, is too far off to get anyone through a server crash.
- **Success surprises the people who get it.** "You put your head down and work on the model train set for 10 years," and "it takes people by surprise when it happens." (@ 6:38). In his view the people who end up famous weren't aiming for it.
- **Chasing the image of a startup is a known failure.** He calls going through the outward motions while neglecting "the one thing that's actually essential which is to make something people want" *playing house*. He also says "Starting a startup is where gaming the system stops working." ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=660s), 2014 @ 7:32, 11:00). A founder chasing fame is likely to optimize for press and how things look, which is the same mistake.
- **Curiosity over careerism.** "be driven by curiosity rather than careerism," and "Ambition tends to make you climb existing peaks, but if you stick close enough to an interesting enough question, it may grow into a mountain beneath you." ([Superlinear Returns](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html), 2023)

**What would change his answer:** if "fame" were really ambition to build something huge that people use. He rates that kind of ambition highly and thinks it's mostly inborn. Then he'd likely say the drive is fine and just aimed at the wrong target: aim at the product and the users, and the recognition will follow. The vault has no statement from him on fame as such, so this part is inferred.

**Verdict:** Paul Graham would most likely be skeptical of "a Web3 social network" as you've phrased it. It names a technology and a category but not a user who badly wants something. He'd tell you to drop the label and answer one question: who wants this so much that they'd use it now, and why? If you and your friends already use a crude version and love it, he'd take it seriously, however odd it sounds. If you picked the idea because Web3 seemed like a big opportunity, he'd call it the kind of idea that sounds plausible and is bad.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: medium). The vault has nothing from PG on crypto, Web3 or decentralized social. `wwxd timeline yc "crypto"` returns 0 statements. The only crypto material is Caldwell and Seibel looking back on Coinbase. So this answer applies his rules about ideas, users and growth to your case.

**How we get there**
1. **Ideas you go looking for tend to be bad but plausible.** "if you make a conscious effort to try and think of startup ideas, you will think of ideas that are not only bad, but bad and plausible sounding." ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 24:34, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1474s). "Web3 + social" is the kind of idea you get by combining two categories on purpose.
2. **The rule behind it** ([[thinking/pg]]): make something people want; understand some group of users so well that you can build exactly what they want. Tricks matter much less than solving the real problem: "There are tricks in the startups, as there are in any domain. But they are an order of magnitude less important than solving the real problem." ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 13:17). In this pitch the chain is the "how", not the "what".
3. **Your case:** the test is whether there is a real group of users who need what decentralization gives them. That could be portable identity, a way around censorship, or creators getting paid directly. If the chain is only there to make the pitch sound fresh, the idea fails his test.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Build for yourself and your friends.** "usually young founders should make something that they themselves want." and "Whatever you and your friends start using now, everyone is going to be using in ten years." ([[web-278ac10fa14b]], https://paulgraham.com/earn.html). If your friends really live in on-chain communities and the current tools frustrate them, that counts in your favour. If not, it counts against you.
- **Token rewards would ruin his main metric.** He asks for the growth rate first because "It shows whether they've built the right thing" ([[web-278ac10fa14b]]). Paying users in tokens to join is the case he warns about: "If your product is a $10 bill that you sell for $5, your growth rate isn't telling you anything useful." ([[web-19ac0b6d18d2]], https://paulgraham.com/powerful.html). He'd also treat it like growth hacks: "Whenever you hear anybody talk about growth hacks, just mentally translate it in your mind to bullshit." ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 10:26).
- **You can't beat Meta or X head-on.** "the way you make a new Google is not by attacking them head on." The opening comes when you "wait for things to change so much that their model is is obsolete" ([[yt-5bxp78i96S8]] @ 3:53–4:28, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=233s). He'd ask what change in 2026 makes the incumbents' model obsolete. Decentralization alone hasn't done that so far.
- **What he would like about it:** network effects. "Network effects make companies more powerful, and I almost always think about how to introduce them." ([[web-19ac0b6d18d2]]). A social network has them built in, so its hard part is getting the first users, not defending later.
- **He wouldn't rule it out because it sounds odd.** "the very best startup ideas tend to sound so lame, at first, that you'd reject them if you were consciously looking for startup ideas." ([[web-278ac10fa14b]]). Caldwell and Seibel tell the same story about Coinbase: "people saw bitcoin as a tiny market that it was going to crash that it was a bubble" ([[yt-Jcuqq48CNj8]] @ 9:50, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=590s; that's Caldwell, not PG). His objection is to an idea that came from looking for an opportunity, not to the technology.
- **He backs founders more than ideas:** "startups' ideas are very mutable" ([[yt-5bxp78i96S8]] @ 20:27). Strong builders with this idea would still interest him. He'd expect the idea to change.

**What would change his answer:** a side project that is already growing quickly through word of mouth, without token incentives, among a group you belong to. Its users would have to want something only a decentralized design gives them, not just put up with it. Then the "Web3" label stops mattering, and his rules ("could this be the real product?", grow and add network effects) all point toward building it.

One gap to keep in mind: PG has posted about crypto elsewhere, but none of it is in this vault, so I haven't used it. To ground the answer in his actual crypto views, add those sources to `vaults/yc` and compile them.

**Verdict:** No. Paul Graham would tell a startup not to spend its seed money on a Super Bowl ad. In his view a startup grows by making something users love and then telling those users about it. You can't buy that kind of growth with mass advertising, and seed money should go toward reaching your next milestone.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: high). The vault has nothing from him on Super Bowl ads specifically. But his rules on growth, money and brand each settle the question, and he has stated them in several sources.

**How we get there**
1. **The nearest case: shortcuts to growth.** He dismisses growth tricks outright: "Whenever you hear anybody talk about growth hacks, just mentally translate it in your mind to bullshit." The way to grow is "to make something that users really love. Right, and then tell them about it." ([Before the Startup](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=626s) @ 10:26). For a startup that is growing, but not fast, his answer is "Do things that don't scale" (@ 44:21). That means recruiting users one by one, which is the opposite of a broadcast ad.
2. **The rule behind it** ([[thinking/pg]]): "you have to have something people want. And you only prosper to the extend that you do" (@ 12:43). Users are the real test. Money spent to put the product in front of 100 million people doesn't make the product something people want.
3. **Applying it to this case:** a Super Bowl ad is the most expensive possible way to tell people about a product before you know they love it. If they don't love it, the ad wastes the money. If they do, you didn't need the ad.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Seed money is for reaching a milestone.** "So you just do what you can on the money you got. As long as you can get to some kind of milestone, then you can convince investors to give you more." ([2026 interview](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=729s) @ 12:09). An ad doesn't produce that milestone. Only traction does.
- **Growth rate matters, not one spike.** He judges startups by growth rate, and ties growth to the customers who grow and decide fastest: "If your growth rate is good enough, the absolute numbers will take care of themselves" ([Making Startups Powerful](https://paulgraham.com/powerful.html)). A one-night burst of signups isn't a growth rate.
- **Heavy advertising is what brand businesses do.** In *[The Brand Age](https://paulgraham.com/brandage.html)* (2026) he describes luxury watches this way: "brands spend a lot on advertising and use tricks to limit supply, and what the buyer gets in return is an expensive status symbol." He concludes that "pushing people's brand buttons is just not a good problem to work on."
